cards.front: Why does each farmer on a shared pasture keep adding animals even when the grass is being overgrazed?
cards.back: Each farmer keeps the full gain from an extra animal, while the damage from extra grazing is spread across all farmers, so each one has a reason to keep adding.
cards.hint: Think about who keeps the profit of one extra animal and who absorbs the harm.

cards.front: How does overuse push a renewable resource toward depletion?
cards.back: When total use is greater than the rate of renewal, the stock shrinks and catches or supplies fall. Users often work harder to compensate, which speeds up **depletion**.
cards.hint: Compare total use with how fast the resource can replace itself.

cards.front: What is the **sustainable yield** of a renewable resource?
cards.back: The **sustainable yield** is the maximum amount that can be harvested indefinitely without reducing the resource's ability to renew.
A **commons** is a resource, such as fish, groundwater, or air, that many people use and no one individual owns or controls.
cards.hint: Think about who owns the village pasture.

cards.front: What do we call the pattern where users following their own short-term interest overuse a shared resource?
cards.back: The **tragedy of the commons**. The resource is depleted or degraded, so everyone ends up worse off.

cards.front: Which shared resource in international waters is overused when many fleets catch the same fish?
cards.back: **Ocean fish stocks**, since many fleets harvest the same fish and the stock can shrink.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to think the tragedy of the commons only affects land resources?
cards.back: It applies to any shared resource, including **air, water, and fish**. Overuse can harm all of them.
cards.hint: Think about what other shared resources people use.

cards.front: Why do shared air and rivers lose quality when many users add waste?
cards.back: They can absorb some waste, but when many users add waste the shared system fills up and its quality drops.
cards.hint: Think about how much a system can take in before it is full.

cards.front: What is a **regulation** used to manage a commons?
cards.back: A **regulation** is a legal rule, made by a government, that limits how a resource may be used and by whom.
cards.hint: Think about who makes the rules.

cards.front: What is **privatization** of a shared resource?
cards.back: **Privatization** is transferring the resource to private owners, who control its use and bear the costs of any damage.
cards.hint: Compare who pays for damage here with a commons.

cards.front: Why is privatization hard to use as a fix for air or the open ocean?
cards.back: Air cannot be split into owned parcels, and the open ocean is also hard to divide, so the owner-pays method is hard to apply.
cards.hint: Think about whether a resource can be divided into pieces.

cards.front: What is the main weakness of regulation as a way to limit overuse?
cards.back: It needs **monitoring and penalties**, because rules fail when nobody checks them.
cards.hint: Consider what makes a rule actually work in practice.

cards.front: What is **community-based management** of a commons?
cards.back: A system in which the users of a resource make and enforce their own rules for sharing it.
cards.hint: Think about who sets the limits instead of a distant government.
